items.description: Everything: the paper theme, fonts, the ink engine and every Looseleaf component. Overwrites your global CSS tokens.
items.docs:
Looseleaf is installed: paper tokens, fonts (Kalam, Caveat, Special Elite, IBM Plex Mono), the ink drawing engine and every component.
Dark mode follows shadcn: add the `dark` class to <html>. A second theme is a `[data-theme="…"]` block that overrides the CSS variables.
Docs and the component list: https://kevintngo.github.io/looseleaf

items.name: accordion
items.title: Accordion
items.description: Ruled rows that open. Each row sits on a hand-pulled pencil rule; a hovered row gets a highlighter swipe, and an opened row turns its chevron over, writes a margin brace beside its text and lets the words soak in. Radix behaviour and keyboard support are untouched.

a11y: The WAI-ARIA accordion pattern from Radix: each trigger is a button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` inside a heading; Enter and Space toggle; ArrowDown, ArrowUp, Home and End move between triggers.
The panel is a `region` labelled by its trigger. Closed panels are removed from the accessibility tree.
The chevron, the rules, the swipe and the brace are aria-hidden and pointer-events: none. State is told by aria-expanded and the turned chevron, not by colour.
Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring round the row; hover-only decoration never carries meaning. Windows high contrast hides the drawings and uses the browser's own focus ring.
Reduced motion (the OS setting or data-motion="reduced") opens rows at once and shows the brace finished.
Right-to-left layouts mirror the brace and text indent; the chevron is symmetric.
meta.usage:
import { Accordion, AccordionContent, AccordionItem, AccordionTrigger } from "@/components/ui/accordion"

export function Example() {
  return (
    <Accordion type="single" collapsible defaultValue="item-1" className="w-full">
      <AccordionItem value="item-1">
        <AccordionTrigger>Is it accessible?</AccordionTrigger>
        <AccordionContent>Yes. It follows the WAI-ARIA pattern.</AccordionContent>
      </AccordionItem>
      <AccordionItem value="item-2">
        <AccordionTrigger>Is it drawn by hand?</AccordionTrigger>
        <AccordionContent>Every line.</AccordionContent>
      </AccordionItem>
    </Accordion>
  )
}

items.name: alert-dialog
items.title: Alert Dialog
items.description: A dialog that asks one question and will not go away until it is answered: no close button, no dismissing by clicking outside, focus starts on the safe answer. For risky questions it can be taped with hazard strips and given a red patch behind its icon.

a11y: Radix AlertDialog: role=alertdialog with `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` (always provide a title and description). Focus is trapped, the page behind is inert, and Escape cancels.
Focus starts on the Cancel button, so an accidental Enter does the safe thing. Clicking outside does not dismiss it.
The hazard tape and the media patch are decoration; the meaning is in the words and in the destructive button (hatched, not only red).
With reduced motion the sheet simply appears; in `calm` density it is flat and untaped.
meta.usage:

  AlertDialog, AlertDialogAction, AlertDialogCancel, AlertDialogContent, AlertDialogDescription,

} from "@/components/ui/alert-dialog"

import { Icon } from "@/components/ui/icon"

items.name: alert
items.title: Alert
items.description: A message on a slip of paper, drawn in felt tip. Default and destructive as upstream, plus info, success, warning and a sticky-note variant. Each tone has its own pattern in the margin as well as its own colour, and a 16 px icon put first is circled in the tone's marker.

a11y: `role="alert"`: assertive live region, announced when it appears. For content that is on the page from the start, override with `role="status"` or `role="note"`.

Tone is told by pattern and icon as well as colour: hatching (destructive), a double rule (info), a marker strip (success), a highlighter panel (warning). Destructive text is red on a paper slip with the faintest red wash, 4.6:1 (the description is not dimmed as upstream's is).
The box, the margin marks and the circle round the icon are aria-hidden and pointer-events: none. The icon is decorative unless you give it a `label`.
Buttons and links inside an alert are their own hosts with their own focus rings.
Calm density draws a single pencil loop and one rule in the tone's colour; Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with a real border.

items.name: annotate
items.title: Annotate
items.description: One component for every mark, in the spirit of RoughNotation: put a highlight, an underline, a circle, a box, brackets, a strike, a cross-out or a scribble on real words, and draw it on when it scrolls into view.

a11y: The words are ordinary text: selectable, copyable, found by search and read in order. Every drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none.
A mark that carries meaning (the right answer, a price that changed) needs the meaning in words as well; a drawing alone is not announced.
Highlight is a <mark>, strike-through is an <s>. Before the drawing exists, without JavaScript, and in Windows high contrast, the browser's own decoration shows instead.
Reduced motion (or data-motion="reduced") zeroes the draw-on: marks simply appear.

items.name: arrow
items.title: Arrow
items.description: A hand-drawn arrow that points where you tell it: one of eight directions inside its own box, or straight at another element on the page. Straight, curved, or with a loop-the-loop, five heads, and an optional label.

a11y: Decorative: the drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none. If the arrow says something ("start here"), put it in text; a label given as children is real text.
It never affects layout: the box is yours, the drawing may spill 14 px beyond it (or as far as the target with pointAt).
Windows high contrast hides the drawing, like every overlay ink; the label stays.
Reduced motion zeroes the draw-on.

items.name: aspect-ratio
items.title: Aspect Ratio
items.description: A box that keeps its width-to-height ratio while its width changes. Exactly shadcn's; the hand-made part is what surrounds it: a photograph on a Polaroid, a print taped at its corners, a map pinned to the desk.

a11y: Layout only: no role, no name, no keyboard behaviour. Give the image inside it real alt text, or an empty alt if it is decoration.
The frames in the examples (a Polaroid's white border, tape, a pin) are decoration and hidden from assistive tech; the caption is real text.
A ratio box has no minimum height, so it collapses to nothing in a container that has no width: give the parent one.

items.name: asterisk
items.title: Asterisk
items.description: Hand-drawn footnote marks: an asterisk, a star, a dagger or a double dagger, in red pencil, sized like a superscript after the word they belong to. Give it a label and an href and it links to the footnote.

a11y: Decorative by default (aria-hidden). With `label` it is role="img" with that name; with `label` and `href` it is a real link (its hit area is 24 px or more).
A footnote mark points at a footnote: keep the footnote in text, and link the two (`href="#fn1"` here and an id on the note).
Sized in em, so it follows the text it sits in. Kept in Windows high contrast as a drawn glyph.

items.name: attachment
items.title: Attachment
items.description: A file handed over in a conversation: a slip clipped to the message, or a print taped up. Five states (idle, uploading, processing, error, done), a pencil progress bar and a remove button. The pencil traces the slip, dashes it while it is only a promise and goes red when it fails.

a11y: AttachmentProgress is a `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuenow`/`min`/`max` (none while indeterminate). Inside an attachment it is named by the AttachmentTitle unless you give it an `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`; on its own it needs one.
An AttachmentTrigger covers the attachment and is the tab stop; the Action buttons above it (z-20) stay separately focusable. Label both: the file name is not enough for 'Remove'.
The state is never only colour: error is red pencil plus a red message plus (for you) a retry action; idle is dashed; done carries a clip.
Sheets, outlines, clips and tape are aria-hidden and take no pointer events. Calm density hides the clip and the tape and traces a plain hairline.
Error text is red on slip (4.8:1); titles are ink on slip (14:1).
A finished chip carries a paper clip over its end. With no action beside it the content keeps clear of the clip (extra end padding), so a long title truncates before it, not under it.

items.name: avatar
items.title: Avatar
items.description: A face, circled in felt tip. The picture is circled by a hand-drawn loop; without one the initials sit on a disc of marker in a stationery colour chosen from the name. A status dot goes on the corner, and a group overlaps its faces and ends in a sketched "+3".

a11y: The loop, the disc and the dot are aria-hidden decoration. Give the picture an `alt` (or `alt=""` next to the name in text), and give AvatarFallback a `name` so the person is read out instead of two letters.
Colour is never the only carrier: the initials say who, and the badge needs its own text for its meaning (online, busy). The initials are ink on a 62% marker, 5.5:1 or better on all eight colours.
An avatar is not interactive. Wrap it in a Button or link yourself, and the hand-drawn loop then sits inside that control's focus ring.
The same name is always the same colour on the server and in the browser (a hash of the trimmed, lower-cased name), so nothing changes at hydration.
Windows high contrast removes the drawings and keeps the picture or initials.

items.name: badge
items.title: Badge
items.description: A small mark that sits next to a word: a marker stamp, a highlighter swipe, a red-hatched warning, a circled word, and a count that can be written as tally marks. Same variants and asChild as shadcn.

a11y: A badge is plain inline text in a span: it is read in reading order with what is around it. Give a status badge words ("Beta"), never only a colour or a mark.
A tally is decoration for the eye; the number is real text in the DOM (visually hidden), so `<Badge tally count={7}>` reads as "7".
Ink on the marker fill is 4.6:1, on the highlighter 12:1; destructive is told apart by its hatch and its word as well as its red.
As a link (asChild), the badge keeps the link's role and href, takes keyboard focus and draws the blue felt ring; hover adds a drop-line, a swipe or an underline and is off on touch screens.
Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with a real 1 px outline. Reduced motion removes the hover tilt and the fill nudge.

items.name: boil
items.title: Boil
items.description: Makes drawn things shiver the way hand-animated line drawings do. About six times a second it moves to the next of a few frames: doodles are redrawn by a new hand, and buttons, cards and fields inside wobble a little differently. It stands still when motion is reduced, off screen and in a hidden tab.

a11y: Boil changes drawings, never content or layout: the shapes do not move, the lines shiver by a fraction of a pixel to a couple of pixels. Nothing is announced and nothing takes focus.

Reduced motion (the OS setting, data-motion="reduced", or an InkProvider with motion="reduced") shows the resting drawing and runs no timer. The same happens while the tab is hidden and while the wrapper is scrolled out of view.

WCAG 2.2.2: a boil that runs for more than five seconds is moving content. It stops for people who ask for reduced motion, but give everyone else a way out where it matters: bind `active` to a pause control or to a preference. Children keep their state, focus and drawn ink across frames (they are re-seeded, never remounted).
Use it for a few live things (a mascot, a logo doodle, a call to action), not lists: every frame re-renders the children. The timer stops when the component unmounts.
Hooks for your own drawings: useBoilFrame() and useBoilSeed(seed) return the frame and a frame-suffixed seed inside a Boil, and the plain seed outside one.

items.name: bookmark
items.title: Bookmark
items.description: A ribbon bookmark you can press. Unpressed, a dashed pencil ghost of a ribbon marks the place; pressed, the woven, edge-stitched cloth ribbon hangs there in its colour and casts a short shadow. It is a Toggle underneath, so `aria-pressed`, Space and Enter come for free. `BookmarkRibbon` is the same ribbon as a page marker with no behaviour.

a11y: Bookmark is a real toggle button: it announces "pressed" or "not pressed", it is reached by Tab and pressed with Space or Enter. Give it a name that says what it saves ("Save this article"); the name does not change with the state, `aria-pressed` does.

items.name: carousel

items.description: Embla's smooth, swipeable scroller with paper furniture: hand-drawn arrows outside the slides (dashed when there is nowhere to go) and, if you want it, a tally under them: one stroke per slide, groups of five with the fifth struck across the other four, the current slide in blue felt. items.name: chart
items.title: Chart

Real text on a real DOM, a keyboard cursor, a tooltip on a slip of paper, a legend that switches series off, a table for screen readers, and a pencil pattern on every series so colour is never the only channel.

a11y: Every chart is one tab stop with arrow-key navigation. The drawing is a `role="application"` with an accessible name, a role description ("bar chart") and a spoken summary; left and right move between data points (up and down between series, or between rows for sideways bars and grids), Home and End jump to the first and last, Escape closes the tooltip. Calm density draws hairlines, no fill offset and 12 px hand text for dense screens. The plot always runs left to right (a time axis does not mirror); the legend and the words on the tooltip follow the page direction.

Label it with <Label htmlFor>, wrap it, or use aria-label. A Label next to it is a peer: peer-disabled dims it, and hovering the label (a Field row with group/field, or a label right after the box) lights the box's hover overlay.

The tick is drawn on with a stroke reveal (0.3 s). Reduced motion (the OS setting or data-motion="reduced") shows the finished mark at once.
Right-to-left layouts need nothing: the box is symmetric and every offset is logical.

items.name: combobox

items.description: A field you can search. Press it and a command list opens on a slip; type to narrow it, arrow keys and Enter to choose. It can be the single-select of the shadcn docs, an editable field, or a multi-select whose choices are hand-drawn hang-tags you can take back; it can offer to create what you typed and wait for results from a server.

Chosen rows say "selected" to screen readers as well as showing a tick. Tags are named "Remove <label>" on their x; Backspace in the empty input removes the last one. In a `multiple` combobox a polite status says what was added or removed (a tag taken back leaves nothing else to hear).

The input's `aria-activedescendant` always names the row that is highlighted, after every keystroke and every arrow key, and is dropped when the list is closed or empty (cmdk records it before it has redrawn the rows, so after typing it named a row that was gone; the same fix is in `CommandInput`).
Pressing a row with the mouse does not pull the focus out of the search box, so you can pick a tag and keep typing (or press Backspace); the x on a tag hands the focus back to the input.
A polite status under the search box says how many results are left; the empty message and the loading row are announced by cmdk's own roles (`progressbar` for Loading).

Nothing depends on hue alone: the highlighted row is a highlighter shape, the chosen row has a tick and a text cue, tags are shapes with a label and a remove button. In Windows high contrast the field gets a real border.
Touch: the trigger is 36 px tall (32 compact, 28 calm), rows 36 px, the tag's x is a 24 px target.

A polite status under the search field says "3 results" or "No results" after each keystroke, which cmdk does not do by itself. The empty message is shown as well.
The highlighted row is a highlighter-yellow shape, not only a hue; a disabled row is graphite and dimmed but still readable.

CommandDialog is a Radix dialog: focus goes into the input and Escape closes. Radix returns focus only to a `DialogTrigger`; a palette opened by a shortcut or a button that sets `open` has none, so CommandDialog remembers who had the focus when it opened and gives it back when it closes, unless the app has moved it on by then (choose a result, go to that page, and the focus stays on the new page's heading instead of jumping back to the button). Arrow keys move the focused note by 8 px (Shift 32 px), R turns it 4 degrees clockwise (Shift+R back, limited to 24), Enter or Space brings it to the front. Notes stay inside the cork.
Where a note ended up is announced politely, once, after the last key press ("Call mum at 56, 30.").

Pointer: notes are picked up anywhere except on links, buttons, inputs and elements marked data-corkboard-nodrag, so a note can hold controls. Escape while dragging with the keyboard focus on the note puts it back.
The focus ring is drawn round the note; it never depends on colour alone. Windows high contrast gives the note a real outline.
Reduced motion: no lift animation, the pin does not pop. Calm density: notes lie flat and the pins are left out.

Resizing: a layout saved on a wide board is drawn inside a narrower one (a note is pulled back in as the cork changes size), while the stored positions are left alone, so widening the board again puts everything where it was saved.

Every note is a tab stop, so a board of fifty notes is fifty Tab presses: keep boards to a handful of notes, or put the board behind a skip link. Touch: a note is touch-action none (a drag on it never scrolls the page), the cork around the notes still scrolls.

items.name: date-picker
items.title: Date Picker
items.description: A date field with a calendar on a slip. Type a date (Sep 17, 2026, 9/17/26, 2026-09-17, tomorrow) or open the calendar and circle one; presets sit in a column beside it; the range version takes two months and closes when you have chosen both ends. Popover + Calendar + Button + Input, composed.

a11y: The typed field is a plain text input (give it a Label or `aria-label`); the calendar button has its own name ("Choose date") and `aria-expanded`, and the slip is a named dialog holding the Calendar, whose keyboard model is react-day-picker's (arrows, Home/End, PageUp/PageDown, Enter/Space).

ArrowDown in the field opens the calendar; Escape closes it and puts focus back on the button; with unsent text Escape drops it. Enter or leaving the field reads what you typed. Pressing Enter on a date that cannot be read does not submit the form it sits in.
An unreadable or disallowed date sets `aria-invalid` (and draws the red box) until the next edit, so the error is not only in colour: the box is also dashed-red with a bang.
With `typeable={false}` the field is one button (`aria-haspopup="dialog"`, `aria-expanded`) whose text is the date or the placeholder.

A single frame draws the focus ring for whichever part has focus (input or calendar button). The slip repeats the InkProvider's density, motion and theme and sits above dialogs, so a DatePicker inside a Dialog works.
Presets are Buttons in a labelled group; ranges are announced by the Calendar's day names ("selected").

items.name: desk
items.title: Desk
items.description: The surface everything else lies on: sage bookcloth under a lamp (linen weave, mottling, a warm vignette), with an optional layer of objects behind your content: a coffee ring, a pencil, paper clips, a ruler, push-pins. Paper is only paper against something darker than itself.

a11y: The desk is a plain element (`div` by default); pass `as="main"` with an `aria-label` if it is your main landmark. Its texture and objects are decoration: aria-hidden, pointer-events-none.
Objects lie behind the content (z-index below every sheet) and are hidden on narrow screens and in calm density, so they never crowd a small or a quiet layout.
Text set straight on the desk must be ink, ink-soft or muted (all at least 4.5:1 on the sage). Windows high contrast replaces the texture with the system canvas.

items.name: dialog
items.title: Dialog
items.description: A modal window that is a sheet of paper dropped on the desk: it lands with a small tilt that settles, the page behind goes dim under a lamp, and the close button is a doodled x. Tape it, pin it, tear its edge; on a phone it becomes a sheet at the bottom of the screen.

a11y: Radix Dialog: role=dialog with `aria-labelledby` (the title) and `aria-describedby` (the description); give every dialog both. Focus moves into the sheet, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle inside it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the trigger.
The page behind is inert while the dialog is open (pointer events off, aria-hidden on siblings) and scroll is locked.
The close button is a real button named "Close"; the x is decorative ink. In Windows high contrast the ink hides and a plain × takes its place.
The drop-in, the fade and the hover blot follow `--ll-motion`: with reduced motion the dialog simply appears. In `calm` density the sheet is flat, untilted and untaped.
Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's `data-density`, `data-motion` and `data-theme`, so density and reduced motion work inside the dialog too.

`modal={false}` works as in Radix: no dim (the sheet sits in a frame that lets clicks through), the page stays interactive and scroll is not locked. Clicking a Sonner toast never counts as "outside", so a toast action pressed over a dialog does not dismiss it. On a phone the bottom sheet pads its foot by `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`, and the dim reserves its scrollbar gutter so the drop-in cannot make a classic scrollbar shove the sheet sideways.

items.name: direction
items.title: Direction
items.description: Tells every Radix part, every drawing and every logical property which way the page reads. One provider at the root of a right-to-left page (or on an island inside a left-to-right one) turns arrow keys, sub-menus, slider edges, tab shoulders and hand-drawn strokes round together.

a11y: Radix reads its direction from this provider only, never from the `dir` attribute. Without it, Tabs, Menubar, Radio Group, Toggle Group, Navigation Menu and the menus keep their left-to-right arrow keys on a right-to-left page, a Scroll Area keeps its scrollbar on the wrong side and a Slider starts at the wrong edge. With it, ArrowLeft moves to the next tab, opens a sub-menu towards the left, and so on.

The wrapper carries `dir`, so the browser lays out bidirectional text, punctuation and inline order correctly; `lang` is yours to set on the wrapper or the page (`<DirectionProvider direction="rtl" lang="ar">`) so screen readers pick the right voice.

Direction glyphs (chevrons, arrows, panel, log-in and log-out, undo and redo, send, list and menu icons) flip themselves in a right-to-left context; icons that do not depend on reading order (check, plus, clock, media controls) stay as drawn.
The drawn layer is aria-hidden and decorative; mirroring it never changes what a screen reader announces.

Two engines behind Looseleaf parts take the direction as an option of their own and do not read the provider yet: give a Carousel `opts={{ direction: "rtl" }}` (Embla) and a Calendar `dir="rtl"` (react-day-picker); a Sonner Toaster follows `<html dir>` or takes its own `dir`. The Direction examples do it.

Kevin Sans covers Latin only. Arabic and Hebrew text falls back to the system font for each missing glyph, which is correct and readable but not hand-lettered; ship an Arabic or Hebrew face in `--font-hand` for a matching look.

items.name: doodle
items.title: Doodle
items.description: Margin doodles: a star, a sun, a flower, a mushroom. Line-led, with one flat fill in register. Use them in the decoration layer, on empty states and in corners of cards.

a11y: Decorative by default; give it a `label` only when it carries meaning that the surrounding text does not.

items.name: drawer
items.title: Drawer
items.description: A slip of paper you pull up from the bottom of the screen (or in from any edge), built on vaul. From the bottom it is torn off a pad along its top edge with a strip of tape as the grab tab; drag it, flick it away, or give it snap points.

a11y: vaul builds on Radix Dialog: role=dialog named by DrawerTitle and described by DrawerDescription, Escape closes, the page behind is inert, and focus returns to the trigger.

Focus moves onto the sheet itself when it opens, not onto the first control (vaul's own default leaves it on the trigger behind the dim, and a field would pop a phone keyboard up over the drawer): a screen reader announces the dialog and Tab starts inside it. Pass `autoFocus` on `Drawer` to jump to the first control instead.

The drawer sits on the same level of the z-scale as dialogs and sheets (`--ll-z-overlay`), so one opened from a dialog stacks above it by open order. A click on a Sonner toast does not count as "outside" and does not dismiss it. On a phone with a home indicator the sheet pads its bottom by `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`.
Dragging is a pointer shortcut only: every drawer also closes with Escape, the Cancel/Close buttons you provide, or a tap on the dim.
The tape is a decorative aria-hidden strip, not a control. With reduced motion the slip simply appears; in `calm` density it is a plain cut slip.

items.name: dropdown-menu
items.title: Dropdown Menu
items.description: A menu written on a slip of paper that drops from a button. The row under the pointer or the keyboard wears the highlighter, a ticked row is a pencil box with a felt-tip tick over it, shortcuts are drawn keycaps, and a destructive row hatches in red pencil instead. Sub-menus, typeahead and focus handling are Radix's.

a11y: Radix DropdownMenu: the trigger has aria-haspopup=menu, aria-expanded and aria-controls; the content is role=menu labelled by the trigger. Rows are menuitem, menuitemcheckbox (aria-checked) and menuitemradio.

Enter, Space and ArrowDown on the trigger open it with the first row highlighted (ArrowUp opens nothing). Up and Down move (pass `loop` to the content to wrap), Home and End jump, typing a letter jumps to the next row that starts with it, ArrowRight opens a sub-menu and ArrowLeft closes it, Enter or Space chooses, Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger. Disabled rows are skipped.

The highlight follows the keyboard as well as the pointer (`data-highlighted`) and is the focus indicator: dark text on the highlighter is 12:1, and because the highlighter itself is faint against the slip, a row with keyboard focus also gets a bar of blue felt at its start edge. A destructive row's cue is the word, the red glyph and the hatch.
Ticks, dots, chevrons and the pencil boxes are aria-hidden drawings. Keycaps are real `kbd` elements; the command glyph carries the name Command.

Rows are 32 px high (28 compact and calm). Nothing depends on hover. Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's data-density, data-motion and data-theme; with reduced motion it appears without the slide and zoom. In forced-colors mode the ticks keep the system text colour and the highlighted row takes the system highlight colours.

items.name: dropzone
items.title: Dropzone
items.description: A patch of paper, stitched round its edge, that files can be dropped on or picked into. It checks type, size and count and tells you why a file was refused; it hands you File objects and shows them in a ruled list with thumbnails and progress lines. It uploads nothing: that part is yours.

a11y: The drop target is a `<label>` round a real `<input type="file">`: the input is a tab stop (visually hidden, never `display: none`), Enter and Space open the picker natively, the label's text is its name (override with `inputProps['aria-label']`), and a screen reader user never needs drag and drop.
Keyboard focus shows the blue ring round the whole patch (the input is inside the labelled host). Drag state is only visual: the drop works for pointer users, the picker for everyone.

Refusals are announced: `DropzoneRejections` is a `role="alert"` with one line per file and reason. The list is a named `<ul>`; each remove button is named "Remove <file>" and hands the focus to the zone when its row goes; a progress line is a `progressbar` with `aria-valuenow`.

The state is never colour alone: over is a thicker blue stitch on yellow with Stubby carrying a parcel; invalid is red stitches, `aria-invalid` and the alert; disabled is pale stitches and a disabled input.
Reduced motion stops the wiggle and the icon's lift. Windows high contrast draws a real dashed border (solid while a file is over).
Touch: the whole patch is the target (at least 160 px tall by default, 128 compact, 96 calm); rows are 40 px with a 28 px remove target.

items.name: empty
items.title: Empty
items.description: What a page says when there is nothing on it yet: media, a title in the script font, a line of explanation and an action. The media can be an icon on a slip of paper, Stubby the pencil stub in one of his poses, or a doodle; a `border` draws the sketched, dashed placeholder frame.

a11y: Empty is a plain group of divs, as upstream; the title is not a heading unless you make it one (put an `<h2>` inside `EmptyTitle`, or give the Empty a role and a name).

Stubby, doodles and the icon tile are decoration (aria-hidden): the title and description carry the meaning. If the state is announced dynamically (search results going to none), put `role="status"` on the Empty.
Ink on paper is 14:1, the muted description 8.9:1. The dashed frame is decoration and carries no information.
Buttons and links in EmptyContent are ordinary controls with their own focus rings.
The frame and the tile are hairline in calm density, and hidden in Windows high contrast in favour of a plain outline.

items.name: envelope
items.title: Envelope
items.description: An envelope on the desk with a stamp, a postmark and address lines. It opens: the flap, which belongs to the back panel, stands up behind, and a letter slides out from between the panels, the front panel hiding its foot. Built on Collapsible, so it has a real trigger, `aria-expanded`, and content that is not in the page until it is out.

a11y: The trigger is a real button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, named by its content: make the name say what opening does ("Read the letter from Ada"). The letter is not rendered until it is open, so a screen reader never meets it twice. Open and closed are not carried by the drawing alone.

Source order is tab order: put `EnvelopeFront` (with its trigger) before `EnvelopeLetter`, so that Tab from the trigger reaches a link or button inside the letter it just opened. The letter clips to its sheet and most of it sits behind the front: keep it to a few lines, a heading and a link, and put long messages on a page the letter links to. With `openOnHover`, a letter that holds keyboard focus stays open when the mouse leaves.
Hover opening is a mouse nicety (`openOnHover`); touch and keyboard always use the trigger. The slide-in is skipped with reduced motion, and the flap simply appears.

The paper, seams, stamp, postmark and flap are aria-hidden decoration. Ink on the kraft is 9:1, and so is the address; the postmark is decoration only. Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with outlines.

items.name: field
items.title: Field
items.description: The words around a control: a label, help text and an error, stacked or in a row, grouped in sets with a legend. It is layout, so the only drawings are the wavy red pencil underline of an error and the hand-drawn card around a choice (a label that wraps a radio or checkbox with its own title and help).

a11y: Field is a role=group; a FieldLabel is a real <label> (use htmlFor + id), so a click on it focuses or toggles the control. Wrap radios and checkboxes in a FieldSet with a FieldLegend so the group has a name.

FieldError is role="alert": it is announced when it appears. Point the control at it with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid, so the control's own box turns red as well (hue is never the only cue: the message, the wavy underline and the bang of the field say it too).

A choice card is one big label: clicking anywhere on it toggles its control, and the checked state is shown by the wash and the felt box, not by colour alone (the radio or checkbox inside shows it too). In Windows high contrast the checked card becomes a Highlight block.

Disabling: set `data-disabled="true"` on the Field (the label goes graphite) AND `disabled` on the control. A `disabled` FieldSet disables the controls natively, but the drawn controls choose their dashed disabled drawing from their own props (or their root's), not from an ancestor fieldset: pass `disabled` to each.
`responsive` uses a container query on the FieldGroup, so it reacts to the width of the form, not of the screen.
Right-to-left: everything uses logical properties; the error underline is symmetric.

items.name: flip-card
items.title: Flip card
items.description: An index card with two sides. It turns over in 3D when you click it or press Space, lifting off the desk on the way; the side you cannot see is inert and hidden from assistive technology. For flashcards, reveals, and anything with a back.

a11y: The trigger is a real <button> with aria-pressed (true while the back shows); Space and Enter turn the card. Give it a name that says what happens ("Show the answer").
The hidden face is inert and aria-hidden, so Tab and screen readers only see the side that is showing.
The default overlay covers the card, so faces should be static text. Faces with links or buttons: trigger={false} and a FlipCardTrigger placed beside them.
The card has a fixed size (h-48 w-72 unless you pass another) and its faces do not scroll: size it (`className="h-64 w-96"`) for the longer face, and keep answers short.
Reduced motion: the card swaps sides without turning or lifting (durations collapse to zero).
The corner arrow and the focus ring are drawn and aria-hidden; the focus ring is the same blue felt as every other control.

items.name: folder
items.title: Folder
items.description: A manila file folder that is also a set of tabs: a row of paper tabs standing on a sheet of the same paper. The active tab is the folder's own colour and runs down into the body, so tab and folder are one piece; the others stand a little lower and darker. It is Radix Tabs underneath.

a11y: Radix Tabs gives the whole pattern: `tablist` / `tab` / `tabpanel` roles, `aria-selected`, `aria-controls`, roving focus with arrow keys, Home and End (Left and Right swap in RTL), and a disabled tab skipped by the keyboard.

The drawn tab paper, the crease and the shadows are aria-hidden. The active tab is also `aria-selected` and bold, so it never depends on colour alone. Tab text is ink: 9:1 on the manila, 7.5:1 on a tab standing behind it.

Windows high contrast replaces the drawn tabs with bordered buttons (the tabs carry a real border until their drawing exists and in forced colours), and the active tab fills with the system highlight colour. The open panel is a tab stop and shows the standard focus ring.

items.name: form
items.title: Form
items.description: react-hook-form wired to the drawn controls, exactly like shadcn's Form. FormControl gives the control its id, aria-describedby and aria-invalid, so an Input, Select, Checkbox or Switch turns red pencil when the field has an error, its label follows, and FormMessage writes the message under it with a wavy red underline.

a11y: FormLabel is a real <label for>, FormControl puts the same id on the control, and aria-describedby points at the description and (while invalid) the message; aria-invalid is set for you.

FormMessage is a

that appears next to the control with its id in aria-describedby, so a screen reader reads it with the control when focus arrives. Wrap it in an element with role="alert" (or use Field's FieldError) if you want it announced the moment it appears.

Not every control can be named by FormLabel's `for`: a Slider (role=slider on a span) or a Rating (a radiogroup) needs `aria-labelledby` pointing at an `id` you give the FormLabel, or an `aria-label`. FormControl's id, aria-describedby and aria-invalid do reach a Slider's thumb, a Rating's group and a RadioGroup's group (whose radios turn red).
Errors do not rely on colour alone: the message text, the wavy underline and the control's own drawn state (red box, a bang on text fields) all say it.
Validation timing is react-hook-form's (`mode`: onSubmit by default, onChange, onBlur ...); the drawn components do not re-render their ink when it changes, only their state layers.
Windows high contrast: the ink is replaced by real borders, and the message gets a wavy text underline.

items.name: handwritten
items.title: Handwritten
items.description: Text that looks written, not typeset: every word sits a hair off the baseline and a touch lighter, by a seeded amount. The words stay real inline text; code, links and forms inside are left exactly as typed.

a11y: The text is unchanged: words are inline spans with real spaces between them, so it wraps, selects, copies and is read as ordinary text.
Elements that must stay exact are skipped: code, pre, kbd, samp, var, links, buttons, inputs, media. Add data-handwritten="off" to any element to opt it (and everything in it) out.
A text-decoration on the element (underline, line-through) is passed on to every word. For a drawn line use Underline or Strike around the text instead: they follow the words when they wrap.
Calm density and reduced motion switch the effect off in CSS (--ll-jitter-k = 0); compact writes it lighter. Never apply it to long reading text: it is for notes, captions, labels and titles.

items.name: highlight
items.title: Highlight
items.description: A highlighter swipe behind real words. The phrase stays text you can select and copy; the swipe follows it line by line when it wraps, in yellow or any stationery colour, and can draw itself on as it scrolls into view.

a11y: The words are ordinary text: selectable, copyable, found by search, read in order. The swipe is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none, so it never takes a click or a selection.
It is a <mark>, so assistive technology that announces highlighted text still does. Text on the swipe stays ink on a translucent tint (about 12:1 on the yellow).

Before the first measure, without JavaScript and in Windows high contrast you get the browser's own <mark> background (system Mark colours in high contrast). With animate the swipe is only drawn once scripts run.
Reduced motion (or data-motion="reduced") zeroes the draw-on: the swipe simply appears.

items.name: hover-card
items.title: Hover Card
items.description: A small polaroid that appears when you rest the pointer on a link or move keyboard focus to it: photo stock with a thick lower margin for handwriting, a degree or two of tilt, and tape if you like. A preview for sighted pointer users, never the only home of anything.

a11y: Radix HoverCard opens on pointer hover and on keyboard focus of the trigger, closes on blur and on Escape, and lets the pointer travel from the trigger into the card. It is not announced to screen readers as a dialog: treat it as a preview of information that is also available by following the link.
Touch: hover cards never open on a tap (Radix ignores touch pointers). The trigger must work on its own as a link; use a Popover when the content needs to be reachable on a phone.
The recess frame and tape are aria-hidden decoration. Give the media an accessible name if it carries meaning.
Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's `data-density`, `data-motion` and `data-theme`; with reduced motion it appears without the zoom.

items.name: icon
items.title: Icon
items.description: Every glyph in Looseleaf is a hand-drawn felt-tip icon, redrawn at each size so a 16 px chevron is a chevron and not a shrunken 24 px one. It takes lucide names, so a shadcn snippet keeps working.

Ink is `currentColor`, so text colour utilities and forced-colors mode work; icons are kept in forced-colors mode.
Status icons differ by silhouette, not only by colour: a triangle warns, an octagon stops, a ring informs, an arc waits.

items.name: index-card
items.title: Index card
items.description: A 3 x 5 card of cream stock with a red header rule and blue lines every 30 px. Header, body and footer parts lay out on the printed rules; the card can have its rod hole punched at the foot, a coloured flag stuck over its edge, and a pile of cards behind it.

a11y: An index card is a plain `div`; use `as="article"` or `role="group"` with a label when it means more. The hole, flag and pile are aria-hidden decoration; put anything a flag stands for into text.
Body ink is 14:1 on the card; the muted footer 8:1. The printed rules and the red header line are decoration and mirror for right-to-left text.
The tilt is zero in calm density; Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with a plain outline.
meta.usage: import { IndexCard, IndexCardContent, IndexCardFooter, IndexCardHeader, IndexCardTitle } from "@/components/ui/index-card" Sources sketchbook, dip pen, ink filed under P12

items.name: input-group
items.title: Input Group
items.description: One hand-drawn field around an icon, some text, a button and the control, so a search box or a URL field is a single box instead of three. The box takes the control's focus, invalid and disabled states, and grows with a textarea. The same parts as shadcn's Input Group.

a11y: The group is role="group"; label the CONTROL (a Label with htmlFor, or aria-label), not the group. Addon icons are decorative; put meaningful text in an InputGroupText or give the button an aria-label.

Focus stays on real controls: Tab goes through the control and the buttons in the DOM order, with the group's blue ring around the box when the control is focus-visible and each button's own ring when it is.

State: `aria-invalid` on the control turns the box red and draws the wavy underline; `disabled` on the control (or `data-disabled="true"` on the group) draws the dashed box. Neither depends on hue alone. Pair invalid with a message and aria-describedby.
Windows high contrast replaces the ink by a real border on the group. The drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events: none.
Right-to-left: addons use logical padding and ordering (inline-start is the right side), the wavy underline mirrors, and nothing else needs a twin.

items.name: input-otp
items.title: Input OTP
items.description: A one-time code as a row of separate hand-drawn boxes. The box that takes the next character wears the blue ring and a blinking pencil stroke; typed characters are written in script; a wrong code turns the boxes red. Underneath is one real input (the input-otp package), so paste, SMS autofill, password managers and the mobile keyboard just work.

a11y: There is one real `<input>` (not six), so name it with a Label (`htmlFor` on the id you pass) or `aria-label`. Screen readers read the code as typed; the boxes are decoration (their drawings are `aria-hidden`).

Typing, Backspace, arrow keys, selection, paste and SMS autofill (`autocomplete="one-time-code"`) are the browser's own; a `pattern` filters what can be typed or pasted. Password managers get room for their badge (`pushPasswordManagerStrategy`).
`aria-invalid` is set on the input when `invalid` is; the boxes turn red with a drawn pencil box, not only a colour change, and a message (`role="alert"`) is yours to add.
The active box has a drawn blue ring and a caret; in Windows high contrast it gets a real Highlight outline. The blink stops under reduced motion (and `data-motion="reduced"`).
Form reset: the code lives in the package's own state, so `<button type="reset">` does not clear it; control the value (`value` + `onChange`) and clear it in your own reset handler.
Touch: boxes are 40 x 48 px (36 x 40 compact, 32 x 36 calm; on a phone card they narrow to about 38 px, never below 24), and the invisible input covers the whole row, so a tap anywhere focuses it.

items.name: input
items.title: Input
items.description: A one-line text field: a pencil box on paper around a real <input>, with blue felt for what you type. It draws its own hover, focus ring, invalid (red pencil and a !), disabled (dashes) and read-only (printed) states.

a11y: A native <input>: label it with <Label htmlFor>, aria-label or aria-labelledby; type, required, pattern, autocomplete and inputmode work as usual.
aria-invalid, disabled and readOnly are the real attributes; the drawing follows them. Pair aria-invalid with aria-describedby pointing at the error text.

Focus draws a blue felt ring (3:1 or better against paper) when the input is focused by keyboard or click (text fields always match :focus-visible). Before the drawing exists and in Windows high contrast the browser's own outline and a real border are used.
The drawing is aria-hidden, pointer-events: none and never focusable. Typed text is blue felt on paper (7:1), placeholders are graphite (6.8:1), disabled text is graphite on a pale wash.

16 px text on every screen size, so iOS does not zoom on focus. Number spinners, the search clear button and the password reveal of Edge are removed; the keyboard behaviour (arrow keys, Escape) is untouched.
Reduced motion: no fade, no wobble; the field has no hover tilt at all.

items.name: item
items.title: Item
items.description: A row for lists of things: an icon or photo, a title with a line of description, some actions. Rows sit on ruled paper, a link row lights up under a highlighter swipe, and none of it carries ink of its own, so a list of hundreds costs nothing.

a11y: ItemGroup is role=list and every Item inside it is role=listitem (upstream leaves that to you, and axe reports the group otherwise). An asChild link or button is wrapped in a listitem, so it keeps its own role, name and keyboard behaviour.

A link or button row is one big hit area. Its focus mark is a plain 2 px blue outline, not the drawn felt ring of a Button (a row carries no drawing, so its ring is CSS too); hover is a highlighter swipe that is also visible without its hue (the swipe changes the background's lightness), and is off on touch screens.
The drawing (outline, rules, wash) is decoration in CSS: it has no role, cannot take focus and does not change layout. In Windows high contrast it becomes a real 1 px border and a real rule.
Muted text is 8.9:1 on paper; the description is clamped to two lines, so put anything essential in the title.

items.name: kbd
items.title: Kbd
items.description: A keyboard key, drawn in pencil as a little keycap with a shaded thickness that presses flat under your finger. Used inline, in groups, in tooltips and in menus.

a11y: Kbd is the semantic <kbd> element: screen readers read the text as it is written. Write words for modifier keys when the symbol would be read unhelpfully ("Ctrl" rather than an icon), or give an icon-only key an Icon with a label (aria-label is not allowed on a bare <kbd>).
Decorative by nature: it is not focusable and has no role. The press animation is pointer feedback only; nothing depends on it.
Muted graphite on paper is 8.9:1. Inside a Tooltip or a menu the label and the drawing take that surface's text colour.
Calm density draws a plain pencil box without the thickness; reduced motion removes the press transition.

items.name: label-tag

items.name: label
items.title: Label
items.description: The words that go with a field, in the bold hand font, with an optional red pencil star for required fields. It fades with a disabled control and hands its click to it.

a11y: A native <label>: clicking it focuses or toggles its control; the control's accessible name is the label's text (the star is aria-hidden).

Bold Kevin Sans at 15 px in ink on paper (14:1). Disabled controls dim their label: put peer on the control before the label (peer-disabled), on a drawn Input / Textarea frame (peer-has-[>input:disabled]), or wrap both in a group with data-disabled="true".
The star is intrinsic art: it stays visible in Windows high contrast and never takes focus.

items.name: lettering
items.title: Lettering
items.description: Display titles in the script font with a riso print look: ink with a second colour printed a hair off register. Pure CSS text-shadow, so the words are real text at any size. No gradients, no filters.

a11y: A real heading (or the element you choose): headings keep their level and outline. The offset colour is decoration; the ink text has 14:1 contrast on paper.
Use one Lettering as the page's h1 at most; for repeated display text prefer p or span.
The riso offset is a text-shadow, so it scales with the text, follows the density knob (calm = none) and disappears in Windows high contrast.

items.name: marker
items.title: Marker
items.description: The pencil line between two days of a conversation, the red one where you stopped reading, and the quiet note that someone joined. A separator, a border or a plain line of small print.

a11y: Markers are plain divs (as upstream). Inside a `role="log"` transcript a separator is announced as its words: 'Today', 'New messages'.
Nothing is conveyed by the drawing alone: the unread state is the words, and colour is backed by the asterisk and the highlighter swipe.
Use `asChild` with a `button` to make 'New messages' a control; the drawn focus ring is the button's own.

Difference from upstream: `markerVariants` gives the layout only. The lines of `separator` and `border` are drawn parts of `Marker` (a pseudo-element cannot hold a drawing), so applying the variants to your own element draws no line.
Ink lines are 3:1 or more against paper; the words are muted text at 8.9:1 (ink on the highlighter swipe 12:1).

items.name: marquee
items.title: Marquee
items.description: A ticker written on a strip of washi tape. The text runs along it, fades at the ends, stops while you point at it or focus inside it, and has a pause button. With reduced motion it is a still strip with the text centred.

a11y: Only the first copy of the text is exposed; every repeat is aria-hidden and inert, so a screen reader reads the ticker once and Tab does not visit links twice.
It pauses on hover and while focus is inside it (WCAG 2.2.2), and the pause button has aria-pressed. The button is on by default; do not remove it for a ticker that moves for more than five seconds.
Reduced motion (the OS setting or data-motion="reduced"): the animation is off, the repeats are hidden and the one copy is centred on the tape.
Put the words that matter in the first copy in the DOM order you want them read; the ticker itself is role="marquee", which assistive technology treats as a non-live region.

Ink on the default orange washi is 7:1 and on the dotted and gingham tapes above 6:1. The text is 24 px semibold script with a paper halo (a CSS text-shadow), so it holds on patterned tape; keep phrases short, and use `masking` when the words are long.
A short phrase on a wide screen is repeated as often as it takes to fill the band (at most 48 copies, all but the first hidden and inert).

items.name: mascot
items.title: Mascot
items.description: Stubby, the pencil stub who does the drawing. He waves in welcomes, thinks in empty search results, sleeps when nothing is happening. An original character drawn as a die-cut sticker: a chubby pencil stub with a face and nothing else (no arms, no legs, no clothes). His mood is his face, a small lean of the body and one doodle floating beside him.

a11y: Decorative by default; the surrounding text ("Nothing here yet") is what carries meaning.

items.name: menubar
items.title: Menubar
items.description: A desktop-style menu bar: a strip of paper with a pencil ruler along its foot and the menu titles written on it. Hovered, focused or open, a title wears the highlighter; each menu opens the same slip as the dropdown. Roving focus, hover-to-switch and typeahead are Radix's.

a11y: Radix Menubar: role=menubar with menuitem titles (aria-haspopup, aria-expanded). Left and Right (mirrored in RTL) move between titles; Enter, Space or ArrowDown opens a menu with its first row highlighted (ArrowUp on a title opens nothing). Once one is open, hovering another title or pressing Left or Right from a plain row switches menus.

Inside a menu: Up and Down move (disabled rows are skipped), Home and End jump, typing a letter jumps to the next row that starts with it, ArrowRight opens a sub-menu and ArrowLeft closes it, Enter or Space chooses, Escape closes and returns focus to the title. The bar is one tab stop.

The strip and its ruler are aria-hidden decoration with no pointer events; the titles keep a 28 px hit box. The highlight follows the keyboard as well as the pointer, and keyboard focus on a title also shows the theme's blue focus ring; inside a menu the row with keyboard focus gets a bar of blue felt at its start edge.

Ticks, dots, chevrons and pencil boxes are aria-hidden drawings; keycaps are real `kbd` elements. Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's data-density, data-motion and data-theme. In forced-colors mode the strip gives way to a real outline and the hovered, focused or open title takes the system highlight colours.

items.name: message-scroller
items.title: Message scroller
items.description: The scrolling transcript of a chat: it opens on the newest message, sticks to the bottom while a reply streams and lets go the moment you scroll up, pins your new message to the top so the reply grows beneath it, holds your place when older messages are added above, and wakes a "jump to latest" button when there is more below. Same parts and hooks as shadcn's message scroller, with the behaviour written in, so no extra package.

a11y: The viewport is a labelled `region` and a tab stop, so a keyboard user can scroll with the arrows, Page keys, Home and End; the transcript inside it is a `role="log"`, which announces additions politely.

Taking over is detected from wheel, touch and scroll keys going toward the start, and from a dragged scrollbar (a scroll the scroller did not make itself; a press on the container, not on a message, while your message is pinned): following and pinning stop immediately and never fight the reader. Scrolling toward the end while you are already there changes nothing, so a stream keeps being followed.

The jump button is `inert` (not focusable, not clickable) while there is nowhere to jump, and has a visually hidden label. Pressing it hands the keyboard to the transcript, so the arrows and Page keys carry on from there instead of restarting at the top of the page.

Every word a streaming reply adds is an addition to the `log`, and a screen reader would read the reply piece by piece. While it streams pass `aria-live="off"` to `MessageScrollerContent` and announce the finished reply once from a separate `role="status"` (the examples do); the `TypingIndicator` covers "someone is writing".

Smooth scrolling and the button's slide are decoration: with `prefers-reduced-motion` (or a `data-motion="reduced"` ancestor) the durations collapse and the jump button scrolls instantly, even though it asks for `smooth`.
The focus ring of the viewport (it is a tab stop) is drawn just inside its edge, because the fade mask would cut a ring drawn outside it.
The page fades at an edge only while there is more to scroll there; the fade is a CSS mask, not a colour.

items.name: message
items.title: Message
items.description: The row of a chat message: an avatar, a column with a header, the bubbles and a footer, aligned to the start or the end. Also MessageText, which sets a reply word by word so streaming text soaks in like wet ink.

a11y: All parts are plain divs (as upstream). Put the transcript in a `role="log"` region, which MessageScrollerContent does for you.

MessageText renders one span per word with normal spaces between them, so copy, paste, find-in-page and screen readers read it as ordinary text. The animation is a CSS one that reduced motion turns off; the words and the caret stay.

Text in a right-to-left script (Hebrew, Arabic...) is not split into words. Such text is one plain span with `dir="auto"`, so the browser orders, joins and shapes it itself (no per-word wobble or soak; the caret stays).
Header and footer are 14 px muted text (8.9:1 on paper).

items.name: native-select
items.title: Native Select
items.description: The browser's own <select> in a hand-drawn frame with a pencil chevron. You keep the platform's popup, mobile picker, typeahead and autofill, and a list of hundreds of options costs nothing. Reach for Select when you want the paper slip.

a11y: It is a native select: role=combobox / listbox, the platform's keyboard (arrows, typeahead, Enter, Escape), its own mobile picker, autofill and form value. Nothing is re-implemented.
Label it with a Label (`htmlFor` + `id`) or `aria-label`. A first option with an empty value reads as a placeholder (graphite text) when it is selected.

The frame follows the select's own state: keyboard focus draws the blue ring, `aria-invalid` the red box, `disabled` the dashed one. The popup itself cannot be styled by any library; only its colours and font are asked for.
The chevron is decorative (aria-hidden) and does not take the pointer, so the whole box opens the list. Windows high contrast replaces the ink by a real border.
Right-to-left: the chevron cell, the divider tick and the bang are on the start side.

items.name: navigation-menu
items.title: Navigation Menu
items.description: A site's top navigation as a strip of index dividers: pencil-sketched tabs standing on a pencil line, the open one lifted and washed with highlighter, the current page filled. Its panel drops from under the strip as a slip of paper that follows the size of what is inside, and a felt-tip underline slides along to the open tab. Hover intent, arrow keys and the motion between panels are Radix's.

a11y: Radix NavigationMenu: a `nav` landmark (give it `aria-label`), a list of items, triggers with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. It is a disclosure pattern, not `role=menu`: panels hold ordinary links.

Hover (with intent delay), click and Enter or Space open a panel; Escape closes it and returns focus to its trigger. Left and Right (mirrored in RTL) move between triggers and links, ArrowDown from an open trigger steps into the panel, and Tab moves through the panel's links and on. Focus leaving the menu closes it.

The current page is `aria-current="page"` and a filled tab, so it does not depend on colour. The sketches, the pencil line, the underline and the highlighter are aria-hidden decoration with no pointer events. Tabs are 36 px high (32 compact, 28 calm).
Touch: a tap opens a panel (hover is not needed). Reduced motion removes the drop, the slide between panels and the underline's glide. In forced-colors mode the drawings give way to real outlines.

items.name: paper
items.title: Paper
items.description: A sheet of paper on the desk: a stock (paper, slip, index card, graph, kraft, sticky notes ...), an edge (cut, torn, deckle, pinked ...), printed rules, a shadow and a small seeded tilt. The sheet turns; your content never does.

a11y: A CSS sheet brings the tooth tiles of its stock itself (one deduplicated `<style>` per tile, in the server HTML too), so it needs no provider. Saturated sticky notes lay a veil of their own colour over the tooth, so orange and pink read as paper, not plaster.

The sheet, its rules, tape and fasteners are decoration: the drawing is aria-hidden, pointer-events: none and never focusable. Paper adds no role; give it one (`as="article"`, `role="region"` with a label) when the content deserves it.
Text is ink on paper (14:1 on paper, 9.4:1 on kraft, at least 9:1 on every sticky note) and stays upright: only the sheet and its rules turn.
Tilt is clamped to --ll-tilt-max and is zero in calm density and in reduced-motion contexts that set it; props are hidden in calm density.
In Windows high contrast the drawn svg (fibre fringe, edge line) steps aside and the host gets a real 1px outline; the paper stays cut to its edge, and tape stays visible.

items.name: peel-corner
items.title: Peel corner
items.description: A page whose corner curls back to show the sheet underneath. Hover the corner to lift it, drag it to peel along a diagonal crease, click or press Enter to open it. For a discount code, a hint, a secret, a P.S.

a11y: The corner is a real <button> with aria-expanded and aria-controls (the sheet underneath). Enter and Space toggle it, a screen reader's activate works, and a drag is only an extra.
What is underneath is inert and aria-hidden while the corner is closed, so it is neither focusable nor read early; once open it is ordinary content.
The corner button is a 56 px square laid over the page's corner: keep links and buttons out of that square, or they cannot be reached with a pointer.
Controlled: if the parent declines a change (`peeled` stays as it was), the corner eases back to what the prop says instead of staying half open.
The hit area is 56 px, bigger than the curl. Dragging back toward the corner closes it; a short pull that never gets half way springs back; pointercancel springs back.
Reduced motion: the corner jumps between rest, open and closed instead of easing. Calm density keeps the flap and the button and trims the flap's shadow to two steps.
The flap and its shadow are drawn art, aria-hidden and click-through; the keyboard focus ring is drawn round the corner button.

items.name: polaroid
items.title: Polaroid
items.description: An instant photograph: a white frame with the thick foot, a recessed square window and a caption in script. Put a real image in the window, or let it draw a little scene in marker and felt tip. Tape it, pin it, clip it, pile it up.

a11y: Give a real photograph its `alt` text as usual; the figure and figcaption name it for assistive technology. A drawn scene is decoration unless you pass `label`.

The frame, window shadow, date stamp, veil, tape and fasteners are aria-hidden and pointer-events-none. The `date` stamp is decoration: if the date matters, say it in the caption or the alt text. Caption ink is 14:1 on the frame.
The developing veil does not run with reduced motion or in calm density's flattened tilt; the picture is simply there.

items.name: popover
items.title: Popover
items.description: A slip of paper set down next to its trigger. It can be held with a push-pin or a strip of tape, given a hand-drawn arrow to point at what it is about, and cut from any stock. Focus moves into it, Escape puts it away.

a11y: Radix Popover: the trigger has aria-expanded and aria-controls; the content is a role=dialog that needs an accessible name (PopoverTitle wired with `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-label`). Focus moves into it on open, Escape and an outside click close it, and focus returns to the trigger.

A popover with no trigger (opened by a menu item or a shortcut, positioned by a `PopoverAnchor`) gives the focus back to whoever had it when it opened: Radix only knows the trigger and would drop the focus on the page. It does not when you clicked somewhere else, when the app has already moved the focus on, or when your `onCloseAutoFocus` prevents the default.
Tab moves out of a non-modal popover into the page as usual; set `modal` on Popover to trap focus.
The pin, tape and arrow are aria-hidden decoration with no pointer events.
Touch: works with a tap like any button; nothing depends on hover.
Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's `data-density`, `data-motion` and `data-theme`. With reduced motion it appears without the slide and zoom.

items.name: progress
items.title: Progress
items.description: A bar somebody hatched in pencil and is colouring in with a marker. The marker is one full-length pass revealed by a CSS clip up to the value, so changing the value is a transition, not a redraw. Without a value it becomes a scribble sliding across. Radix Progress underneath.

a11y: role="progressbar" with aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and aria-valuenow (omitted while indeterminate); Radix also sets data-state, data-value and data-max. Give it a name with aria-label or aria-labelledby; use aria-valuetext for "Step 2 of 5" style text.
It is a status display, not a control: not focusable. Put the percentage in text next to it if people need the number; screen readers get it from aria-valuenow.

The drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events: none. The hatch shows how much is left even when the marker's hue is hard to tell; in Windows high contrast the ink is replaced by a real border and a Highlight fill.
Reduced motion (the OS setting or data-motion="reduced"): value changes jump instead of gliding and the indeterminate scribble stops, sitting still in the middle of the bar.
Right-to-left: the marker grows from the right and the indeterminate window slides right to left.

items.name: prompt-input
items.title: Prompt input
items.description: The composer of a chat: a napkin strip with a writing line, an auto-growing textarea, room for attachments and a paper-plane send button that flies off when the message goes. Enter sends, Shift+Enter breaks the line, IME composition is left alone, and while a reply streams the button becomes a stop button. Slots for slash commands and @mentions, with no data of their own.

a11y: Enter and Shift+Enter behave like every chat box; neither fires while an IME composition is open (`isComposing`, the composition events and the Safari keyCode 229 quirk are all checked).

The textarea is named "Message" unless you label it (`aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or an `id` for a `<label htmlFor>`): a placeholder is not a name. While a suggestion list is open it exposes `aria-controls` and `aria-activedescendant`; the list is a `listbox` of `option`s with `aria-selected`.

The submit button is named 'Send message' and, while busy, 'Stop generating' (and then it is a real `type="button"`). The form is deliberately not `aria-busy` (some screen readers would skip the textarea and the Stop button); it carries `data-status`. If the keyboard is on Stop when the reply ends, the focus moves back to the writing line.
Status and errors are yours to announce (a live region in the chat); the composer keeps focus in the textarea after a send.
The paper plane's flight is decoration: with reduced motion the animation ends on the plane at rest. Ink on the napkin is 14:1, the placeholder is graphite (5.9:1).

items.name: quote
items.title: Quote
items.description: A pull quote with big hand-drawn quotation marks and an attribution. A real figure, blockquote and figcaption, with marker or felt marks drawn in the gutters: an opening pair at the top, a closing pair at the bottom.

a11y: Real semantics: <figure> > <blockquote cite> + <figcaption>. Assistive technology announces a quotation and its source.
The quotation marks are drawings (aria-hidden), not characters in the text, so they are not read aloud or copied with the words.
The marks live in the blockquote's padding and never overlap the words; RTL mirrors the whole drawing.
Reduced motion zeroes the draw-on.

items.name: radio-group
items.title: Radio Group
items.description: Pick exactly one. Each choice is a hand-circled ring; picking it colours the dot in with a terracotta blot and writes a felt spiral into it. Radix Radio Group underneath: roving focus, arrow keys, form value, orientation and direction.

a11y: role="radiogroup" with role="radio" items and aria-checked. Tab enters the group at the chosen radio (or the first), arrow keys move AND choose, Space chooses the focused radio (Radix roving focus). Give the group a name with aria-label or aria-labelledby (a fieldset legend works too).

Label each radio with <Label htmlFor>, wrap it, or use aria-label. A Label beside it is a peer: peer-disabled dims it, and hovering the row (a `group/field`) or the label right after the radio lights the ring's hover overlay.
The hit area reaches 8 px past the ring on every side (an ::after, so layout never moves): 32 px for the 16 px ring.
Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring; the drawing is aria-hidden, pointer-events: none and never focusable. Windows high contrast replaces it by a real border and the Indicator shows a real dot.
The chosen state is a filled dot, not only a colour: a bold blot with a dark spiral. Reduced motion shows the finished dot at once.
Right-to-left needs nothing: the ring is symmetric and every offset is logical. Pass `dir="rtl"` to mirror the arrow keys.

items.name: rating
items.title: Rating
items.description: Stars, hearts or suns somebody drew, where you pick how many are filled. Hover previews, half steps are optional, and it is a real radio group (arrow keys, form value), or a plain read-only display with a text alternative. New in Looseleaf: shadcn has no rating.

a11y: An interactive rating is a radiogroup of role="radio" buttons, named "3 of 5" (or with `getLabel`), with aria-checked on the chosen value and a roving tabindex: Tab lands on the chosen glyph (the first when there is none). Name the group with aria-label or aria-labelledby.

ArrowRight / ArrowUp add a step, ArrowLeft / ArrowDown remove one (left and right swap in right-to-left), Home goes to the first step and End to the last; the arrows choose as they move, like native radios. Enter and Space press the focused radio. There is no way to arrow down to 0: use `clearable` and click the chosen glyph, or a Clear button.
With `allowHalf` there are two radios per glyph, one over each half, so a half star has its own name ("3.5 of 5") and its own hit area; pointer previews show the half under the pointer.
A read-only rating is role="img" with a text alternative ("Rated 4.5 out of 5", or your aria-label) and its glyphs are decorative. Put the number in text next to it as well when it matters.
Inside a Form, FormLabel's htmlFor cannot name a radiogroup: give the Rating an aria-label, or aria-labelledby with an id on the FormLabel.
Half steps make narrow targets (half a glyph wide): on touch screens prefer whole steps, or `size="lg"`.

The preview follows the mouse only (not touch, where hover does not exist). The filled and empty glyphs differ in fill and in outline weight, not in hue alone; in Windows high contrast each glyph shows a text star (filled, empty or half).
Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring around the glyph. Reduced motion removes the little bounce under the pointer.

items.name: receipt
items.title: Receipt
items.description: Thermal till paper: pinked (or perforated, or torn) at both ends, printed in the typewriter font, its lines a description list, its total circled in red felt tip by whoever checked it, ending in a barcode made from the number under it.

a11y: A receipt is a plain `div` by default, and a name on a `div` is ignored by screen readers: pass `as="article"` (it is a self-contained document) together with `aria-label`, as the examples do.
The lines are a real description list, so a screen reader hears each item with its price. The total is a list of its own, with the same structure.

The barcode is `role="img"` named `Barcode <number>`; the number is also printed as text. The circle round the total, the pinked ends, tape and clips are aria-hidden decoration: the amount is text either way.
Ink on the receipt stock is 14:1; the footer is 8:1. The type font is set at 13 px on a 20 px line. Windows high contrast replaces the drawn ends with an outline.

items.name: resizable
items.title: Resizable
items.description: Panels you can drag apart. The seam between two panels is stitched by hand, gets a paper tab with a grip if you ask, darkens under the pointer and is pulled tight into one blue line while you drag. Built on react-resizable-panels 4: keyboard resizing, collapsible panels and persisted layouts included.

a11y: The handle is a `role="separator"` with `aria-orientation`, `aria-valuenow` / `aria-valuemin` / `aria-valuemax` and `aria-controls` (the primary panel), and is in the tab order. Give it an `aria-label` that says what it resizes.

Arrow keys move it by 5%, Home and End jump to the limits, Enter collapses or restores a collapsible panel, all from react-resizable-panels. Dragging works with mouse, touch and pen; the hit area is larger than the drawing (at least 24 px for a mouse and 37 px for a finger; the group asks the library for that through `resizeTargetMinimumSize`, which you can override).

ArrowLeft / ArrowRight shrink / grow the first panel whatever the reading direction (react-resizable-panels does not mirror them), so on a `dir="rtl"` page the handle moves against the arrow. Up / Down are exact in a vertical group.
The stitches, the tab and the blue line are aria-hidden decoration; the grip glyph is decorative too.
Keyboard focus draws a blue ring round the middle of the seam (round the tab, when there is one). Windows high contrast draws a real outline round the handle.
Hover, dragging and focus each show without hue: the stitches darken, the seam becomes one continuous line, the ring appears.

items.name: reveal
items.title: Reveal
items.description: Holds its children back until they scroll into view, then draws them on: a wipe along the line, wet ink drying, a sheet dropped on the desk, a stamp, a toss. Direct children can arrive one after another. Without script, and with reduced motion, everything is simply there.

a11y: Hiding is opacity only: the content stays in the accessibility tree and in the tab order the whole time, so it is never withheld from assistive technology or from find-in-page.

The server sends the content visible and unarmed; only after mounting (and only if motion is allowed and IntersectionObserver exists) does it hide and wait. Without script, in old browsers, and with reduced motion (the OS setting, data-motion="reduced" or an InkProvider with motion="reduced") nothing is ever hidden.
Each effect uses one of the theme's --ll-dur-* tokens, so a reduced-motion context collapses the duration to zero.
Do not wrap content people need at once (above the fold, error messages, focus targets). It is for things that arrive with a flourish as you read down a page.

items.name: ribbon
items.title: Ribbon
items.description: A ribbon label: a band of coloured paper with words on it, folded ends and all. For a section heading, a New flag on a card, a price label or a call to action.

a11y: The words are real DOM text on a plain span; the drawing is aria-hidden, ignores the pointer and never affects layout.
With asChild the ribbon is whatever you gave it: a link or a button, with its own role, keyboard behaviour and name. Focus-visible draws a blue ring round the whole ribbon, tails included.
Ink text on each offered tone is at least 4.5:1 (marker 4.6 on its drawn fill, lemon and highlighter 12+). Windows high contrast hides the drawing and gives the element a real outline.

Hover lifts a link ribbon 1 px, draws a drop-line under it and underlines its words, so it is visible without hue. Reduced motion makes the lift instant. Calm density draws a hairline outline and a single-pass fill.

items.name: scribble
items.title: Scribble
items.description: Words scribbled out with tight back-and-forth strokes, like a note someone changed their mind about. A look, not a redaction: the text underneath stays in the DOM.

a11y: Never scribble out a secret: the text is still in the DOM, still selectable, still read by a screen reader. Remove sensitive text from the page instead.
The drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none. Before it exists, and in Windows high contrast, the browser's own line-through is shown.

items.name: scroll-area
items.title: Scroll Area
items.description: A scroll container whose bar is a pencil "scroll mark": a graphite pull sliding down a faint gutter, gone over once more when a hand is on it. It fades in on hover or scroll, works in both directions, and is Radix underneath.

a11y: Native scrolling: wheel, touch, keyboard (arrows, Space, PageUp/PageDown, Home/End) and scrollbar-less devices all work; the mark is an overlay for pointers and never the only way to scroll.

A scroll region with nothing focusable in it is reachable by keyboard in current browsers; the viewport draws a blue ring inside its edge when focused. If yours is not, give the content `tabIndex={0}` and a name.
The gutter and thumb are aria-hidden drawings; the thumb can be dragged and the gutter clicked, as in Radix.
Windows high contrast draws the thumb in the system text colour. Reduced motion removes the fade.
Right-to-left content puts the vertical mark on the left: pass `dir="rtl"` to the root, as Radix asks.

items.name: seal
items.title: Seal
items.description: Rosettes, scalloped seals, medals, ringed seals with rim lettering and wax seals, drawn like the stickers without the white edge. Use one as a verified mark beside a name, an award on a card, or the stamp of approval on a certificate.

a11y: The svg is role="img" named by its words; give `label` for the meaning ("Identity verified") and `decorative` when the surrounding text already says it.
A drawn check or star reads at 16 px, but never carry a status by the seal alone: put the word in the DOM next to it or in `label`.
Windows high contrast keeps the seal (intrinsic art).
The ring lettering is decoration inside the image; the name is what a screen reader gets.

items.name: select
items.title: Select
items.description: A drop-down field. The trigger is a pencil box with a tick before its chevron; the list is a slip of paper set down over or under it, where the row you are on gets the highlighter and the chosen row is bold with a blue tick. Radix Select underneath: typeahead, keyboard, form value, item-aligned or popper placement.

a11y: The trigger is a role=combobox button with aria-expanded and aria-controls; the list is a role=listbox with role=option items (aria-selected on the chosen one). Radix handles everything else.
Enter, Space, ArrowDown and ArrowUp open it. Arrow keys, Home and End move the highlight, letters jump by typeahead, Enter or Space chooses, Escape closes and puts focus back on the trigger.
Give the trigger a name with a Label (`htmlFor` + `id`) or `aria-label`; SelectValue's text becomes its value.
With `name` (or inside a form) Radix keeps a hidden native select in sync, so the value is in FormData and `required` blocks the submit.

The drawing is aria-hidden and never takes the pointer. The highlight does not depend on hue alone: the row also sits on a highlighter shape and the chosen row is bold with a tick. In Windows high contrast the trigger gets a real border.

Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's `data-density`, `data-motion` and `data-theme`, and sits above dialogs so a Select inside a Dialog works. Reduced motion shows the list without the slide and zoom.
Right-to-left: the chevron cell, the divider tick and the bang move to the start of the field, and the tick of the chosen row follows.

items.name: separator
