items.name: sheet
items.title: Sheet
items.description: A notebook page that slides in from the edge of the screen. It is bound along the edge that faces the middle: spiral wire through punched holes, three binder holes, a perforated tear line, or torn out of a pad. Good for settings, filters, carts and mobile navigation.

a11y: Radix Dialog: role=dialog named by SheetTitle and described by SheetDescription. Focus moves in, Tab cycles inside, Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger; the page behind is inert and scroll is locked.

A click on a Sonner toast does not count as "outside" and does not dismiss the sheet. In a right-to-left page the x steps in from the corner when the coils are on the physical left edge; the coils themselves are physical, like the `side` prop. A top or bottom page is capped at 85dvh: give tall content a `min-h-0 flex-1 overflow-y-auto` child.
The coils, holes and torn or perforated edge are aria-hidden decoration with no pointer events; the close button is a real button named "Close" (a plain × in Windows high contrast).
Slide and fade durations follow `--ll-motion`, so with reduced motion the page just appears. In `calm` density the coils are hidden and the page is a plain cut sheet.
Side sheets are physical (`right` is the right edge) as upstream; pass `side="left"` for right-to-left layouts.

items.name: sidebar
items.title: Sidebar
items.description: An order pad hung from the top of the screen: cream paper with a torn top edge and a binder clip. Rows carry their own line of the pad's ruling, hover is the highlighter, and the current page is marked with a highlighter swipe and a bracket in the margin. It collapses to icons or slides away, becomes a sheet on phones, and stays cheap for a long menu: only the one active row draws anything.

a11y: The sidebar adds no landmark of its own: wrap it in a `nav` (or give it `aria-label` on the Sidebar's container) so screen readers can find it. The rows are ordinary buttons and links in a list; `isActive` on a link (`asChild`) or a sub-menu button sets `aria-current="page"` for you (pass your own to override; a plain button gets none); the drawing is decoration.

Ctrl or Cmd + B toggles it from anywhere; the SidebarTrigger is a labelled button ("Toggle Sidebar"). The rail is not a tab stop. On phones the pad opens in a Sheet: a dialog named "Sidebar" that traps focus, closes with Escape or a tap on the scrim and gives focus back to whatever opened it (Radix only does that for its own Trigger, so the Sidebar remembers the opener itself). Growing the window past the phone width closes the sheet, so it does not come back by itself when the window shrinks again. Ctrl/Cmd+B is left alone when something nearer (a rich-text editor's Bold) has already handled the key.

Keyboard focus on a row shows the highlighter and the theme's blue focus ring. Every row is at least 28 px high (32 by default); collapsed rows are 32 px squares, named by their tooltip and their text (keep the label in a `span` so it stays in the accessible name).
When it collapses to icons the labels are hidden with CSS only, so the accessible names stay. Tooltips appear on hover and keyboard focus, never on touch.

The torn edge, ruled lines, binder clip, bracket and sub-menu line are aria-hidden decoration with no pointer events. In forced-colors mode the clip is hidden and the drawings give way to real outlines. Reduced motion collapses the slide of the pad and the fade of the labels.
The open state is remembered in the `sidebar_state` cookie; read it on the server to render the right state on first paint.

items.name: signature-pad
items.title: Signature pad
items.description: Sign on the screen. One brush pen with real pressure, a pencil baseline with its x, a clear button, and a typed-name fallback that is set in hand lettering. It carries the image in a hidden field, so it works in a plain form and can be required.

a11y: The canvas is a named application ("Signature"); the same keyboard drawing as Sketchpad works: arrows move a cursor, Space puts the pen down and lifts it. Typing the name is the accessible alternative and is one button away.
Type mode replaces the canvas by an image named "Signature, typed: Ada Lovelace" and a text field labelled "Type your full name".

Required: a visually hidden text input holds the value so the browser's own validation and message apply; the failure also shows a role="alert" line and moves focus to the canvas (the name field in type mode).
The baseline turns red pencil when invalid, and the message says why (colour is never the only cue).
Windows high contrast keeps the ink colours of the strokes; the sheet gets a real border.

items.name: signature
items.title: Signature
items.description: A name signed in the script font with the pen's flourish under it: a swoosh with a loop that flicks up past the last letter. The name is ordinary text; the flourish is a drawing that can write itself on.

a11y: The name is real text in the page, read by a screen reader; the flourish is aria-hidden. A signature is not proof of anything: say who signed in text if it matters.
The name text is not clipped by the flourish; the drawing spills 20 px beyond its box and never takes a click.
Reduced motion zeroes the signing animation.

items.name: skeleton
items.title: Skeleton
items.description: A placeholder someone sketched in pencil: a pale hatch inside a rough ruled outline that boils gently between three redrawn frames. It costs no ink per instance, so a page of hundreds is as cheap as one.

a11y: A skeleton is an empty element, invisible to assistive tech, as shadcn's. Mark the region that is loading with aria-busy="true" (and a status or a visually hidden "Loading" for screen readers), and remove the skeletons when the content arrives.
Nothing in it is interactive or focusable; the boil is decoration, and a page of skeletons never announces anything.
Reduced motion (the OS setting or the in-app calm-ink setting) and calm density hold the first frame still.
In Windows high contrast the drawing is replaced by a dashed system-colour outline.
The masks need CSS mask-image (every current browser); the stylesheet is injected with <style href precedence>, so React 19 hoists it, dedupes it and includes it in server HTML.

items.name: sketchpad
items.title: Sketchpad
items.description: A real drawing surface. Pointer, touch, pen pressure or the keyboard put strokes on paper, and every stroke is rendered by the interface's own pen (variable-width ribbons, pooled ends, felt / graphite / marker grain), so what people draw looks like the rest of the page. Undo, redo, export as svg, replay.

a11y: The canvas is role="application" (aria-roledescription "drawing canvas") with a name and a description of the keys; the drawn strokes are aria-hidden. Read-only, it is an image named "Drawing, N strokes".

Keyboard drawing: arrow keys move a cursor (Shift = 32 units, Alt = 2), Space or Enter puts the pen down ("Pen down.") and lifts it ("Stroke added."), Escape cancels the stroke or hides the cursor. Leaving the canvas lifts the pen.

Focus: Undo, Redo and Clear disable themselves when they have nothing left to do; if one of them had focus, focus moves to the canvas instead of falling to the top of the page. Every part composes its own `onClick` with the built-in action (call `event.preventDefault()` to cancel it).

Shortcuts on the focused canvas: F felt, B brush, P pencil, M marker, H highlighter, E eraser (only tools that are offered), [ and ] change the width, Ctrl/Cmd+Z undo, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redo.
Tools, colours and widths are radio groups (Radix): Tab enters a group, arrow keys move and select. Every swatch has a colour name; toolbar buttons are at least 28 px with a bigger hit area.
Adding, erasing, undoing and clearing are announced politely ("Stroke added. 3 strokes.").
Windows high contrast: the strokes keep their own colours (forced-color-adjust: none), the toolbar gets real outlines. Reduced motion: replay shows the finished drawing at once.

Touch: the canvas sets touch-action: none so drawing never scrolls the page. That also means a canvas that fills the screen on a phone traps the scroll: leave a margin around it, or put it in a tab or dialog. Palm rejection: a finger is ignored for 1.5 s after the pen was last seen near the screen (and a palm that got there first is dropped when the pen lands), so a person who switches between pencil and finger is never locked out.

Scale: a stroke is stored as thinned points (samples closer than 0.8 units are held back) and drawn by the pen as ribbons, which is about 15 to 30 KB of svg for a hundred points and up to 1 MB for a very long scribble; the finished markup is cached (bounded by size, 24 MB) and a live stroke is previewed with at most 480 points. A page with many hundreds of long strokes belongs in the replay/export flow (toSVG), not in a live canvas.

items.name: slider
items.title: Slider
items.description: Pick a number, or two, by dragging a paper knob along a hand-ruled groove. The range is one marker pass drawn full length and revealed by a CSS clip, so nothing is redrawn while you drag. Ticks, a highlighter or blue-felt range, vertical, and range sliders. Radix Slider underneath.

a11y: Each thumb is a role="slider" with aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuenow and aria-orientation. Arrow keys move by one step, Page Up / Page Down and Shift+Arrows by ten, Home and End go to the ends (Radix; the arrows follow the reading direction in RTL).

Name it. With one value put aria-label or aria-labelledby on the Slider and it lands on the thumb (the Root is a plain span, so a name there would name nothing). With several values the Root becomes a role=group carrying that name, and the thumbs keep Radix's "Minimum" and "Maximum".
Pointer: dragging the thumb or pressing anywhere on the groove works, on touch too (touch-action: none on the slider); the thumb's hit area is larger than the drawing.

The drawing is aria-hidden, pointer-events: none and never focusable. Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring around the knob. Windows high contrast replaces the ink by real boxes (a bordered groove, a Highlight range, a solid knob).
The value is not shown by the slider: pair it with an <output> or text next to it, as the examples do.

In a react-hook-form Form, FormLabel's htmlFor cannot name a slider (a span with role=slider is not a labelable element): give the FormLabel an `id` and the Slider `aria-labelledby` with it, as the Form "Every control" example does. FormControl's aria-describedby and aria-invalid do reach the thumb.
A non-finite value (NaN) is held at `min`. Form reset: a name'd slider goes back to its defaultValue and the range follows.

items.name: sonner
items.title: Sonner
items.description: Toasts as slips of paper tossed onto the desk. A guest check for success, a pink sticky for errors, yellow for warnings, blue for news; stacked, swipeable, with drawn icons, action buttons, promise toasts and tape or a pin to hold them down. Built on the sonner package: you keep its `toast()` API.

a11y: Sonner renders a polite aria-live region (`aria-label="Notifications alt+T"`); Alt+T focuses it so a keyboard user can reach the toasts, and hovering or focusing pauses the timers. Each type is its own icon shape and paper (guest check, pink, yellow, blue sticky), so colour is never the only signal.

Action and cancel are real buttons at least 24 px tall; the close button is named "Close toast". Keep toast text short and never put the only copy of an error in a toast that disappears: pair it with an inline message.
Swipe to dismiss is a pointer shortcut only (sonner); every toast also closes with its close button, its action, its timer or `toast.dismiss()`.
The toss-in uses the theme's `ll-toss` (`ll-drop` when the stack is not on the right) and collapses to nothing with reduced motion. In `calm` density the slips lose their tilt, tape and pin.
Toasts are above dialogs and popovers on the z-scale and stay clickable while a modal is open.

items.name: spinner
items.title: Spinner
items.description: A pencil that will not stop scribbling: a hand-wound spiral whose line is drawn and undrawn round and round, in the colour of the text around it. Still, and whole, when motion is reduced. Stubby can write instead, in three frames like a flip book.

a11y: Like shadcn's, it is role=status with aria-label="Loading": a polite live region that announces its name when it appears. Put a visible word next to it when you can ("Saving...").
The drawing is aria-hidden. It uses the current text colour, so it is as visible as the text next to it (in a disabled button that is the disabled text colour).
Reduced motion (the OS setting, or the in-app calm-ink setting) stops the slide and shows the whole scribble, standing still; Stubby holds his last frame, the finished scribble.
In Windows high contrast the drawing is kept (it is art, not a border) and takes the system text colour.

items.name: squiggle
items.title: Squiggle
items.description: A hand-drawn divider: a wave, a zig-zag, a row of loops, scallops, dashes or dots, drawn to fit whatever width or height you give it. Same semantics as a separator.

a11y: Decorative by default (role="none"), like Radix's Separator; pass decorative={false} to expose it as a separator (with aria-orientation) between sections that really are distinct.
The drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none; it is redrawn when the box is resized. Windows high contrast hides it (a decorative divider loses nothing).
Cost grows with length: about 3 KB for 420 px in a single pull; keep very long dividers (over 1200 px) to `dots` or `dashes`.

items.name: stamp-button
items.title: Stamp button
items.description: A button that is a rubber stamp: a wooden knob on an inked die, in the colour of the impression it will leave. Press it and APPROVED, PAID or VOID lands on the page with a thump. The stamps on a page are JSON, so they can be state.

a11y: The tool is a real button named by its label; Enter and Space stamp exactly like a click. Outside a StampSurface it stamps on itself, so it still does something.
Each impression is an image named by its words (role=img, "Approved"), so the stamped state is in the reading order; a polite status line says "Approved stamped." once per strike.

Only a stamp struck now lands with the thump: impressions restored from saved JSON, a defaultValue or the server's markup are simply on the page, so a reload does not stamp everything again. The thump is an enter animation on the impression and a 2 px give on the page; with reduced motion (the OS setting, data-motion="reduced", or the provider) the impression simply appears and the page holds still.

The drawn tool is decoration (aria-hidden); its label is DOM text on the die at 4.5:1 or better; focus draws a ring round the whole tool, knob included. Windows high contrast hides the drawing and gives the button a real outline.
Do not carry the decision by colour alone: the impression says the word, and the label says what pressing does.

items.name: stamp
items.title: Stamp
items.description: A rubber stamp: solid ink pressed through a worn pad, double-rule border, typewriter capitals, a slight tilt and sometimes the ghost of a first impression. For APPROVED, PAID, DRAFT and friends.

a11y: The svg is an image named by its text (`role="img"`), so a stamped APPROVED is announced as "Approved".

items.name: stepper
items.title: Stepper
items.description: A number you can nudge: minus, the value, plus. One hand-drawn box with a tick before each button, the number in script, buttons that repeat while you hold them, arrow keys and PageUp / PageDown for the keyboard, and a rattle of the box when there is nowhere left to go. The value is a real text input, so it types, pastes and submits with a form.

a11y: The number is a text input with `role="spinbutton"` and `aria-valuenow / valuemin / valuemax / valuetext` (the APG pattern), so screen readers announce it as a number field; ArrowUp / ArrowDown, PageUp / PageDown, Home and End work as the pattern says. Give it a name (a Label with `htmlFor`, or `aria-label`).

The buttons are not in the tab order (as in the APG spinbutton: the input takes the keyboard) but they are real buttons, so a pointer, a switch and a screen reader's activate (a click with no pointer) step once each. Name them for what they change.
A button with nothing left is `aria-disabled`, not `disabled`; pressing it rattles the box (a visual cue that goes with the state, not instead of it) and the number's `aria-valuenow` stays.
Holding a button repeats; releasing (or leaving, or blur) stops, and so does reaching a bound. No motion depends on it: reduced motion turns the number's tick and the box's rattle off.
The wheel is opt-in, and only acts while the number has focus.
Hit areas are the whole cell (36 px, 32 compact, 28 calm), the drawn ticks and box are `aria-hidden`; in Windows high contrast the box gets a real border.

items.name: sticker-board
items.title: Sticker board
items.description: A page you can stick stickers on: drag them anywhere, turn them, size them, stack them, with the pointer or the keyboard. The value is plain JSON ({ id, name, x, y, rot, scale, z }) and it exports to one standalone SVG.

a11y: The canvas is a named group; every sticker is a focusable group with aria-roledescription "sticker", the picked one carries aria-current, and one line of instructions describes them all.

Keys on a focused sticker: arrows move it 8 px (Shift 32, Alt 1); [ and ] (or R and Shift+R) turn it 5 degrees (Shift 15); + and - size it; 0 sets it upright at full size; PageUp and PageDown move it through the stack (Shift goes to the front or the back); Ctrl or Cmd D duplicates; Delete or Backspace removes it and moves focus on; Escape lets go.
Every change is announced politely, once, after the last key press ("Rocket at 216, 150.").

The turn ring and the size square are pointer handles only (aria-hidden); the keys and the toolbar do the same. Shift while turning snaps to 15 degrees. Deleting from the toolbar moves focus to the bare page with nothing picked (the button that was pressed is disabled by then), so a second press cannot take the next sticker.
A read-only or disabled board has no keys, so it offers no instructions: its stickers are named groups and nothing more.
The frame and the focus ring are drawn; Windows high contrast gives the picked sticker a real outline.
Reduced motion: the small growth on hover is instant. Calm density: stickers do not grow on hover and the frame is drawn thinner.

items.name: sticker-picker
items.title: Sticker picker
items.description: A popover of stickers to choose from: a search field, category chips and a grid you walk with the arrow keys. Reach for it in a comment box, a reaction bar or a profile editor. The highlighted sticker peels its corner.

a11y: The search field is a combobox (aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-autocomplete="list") and keeps focus; the grid is a listbox of options that the field points at with aria-activedescendant, grouped by category (role group, named by its heading).

Arrow keys move the highlight: Left and Right one sticker, Up and Down one row (a row is `columns` wide; between categories the column is kept as far as it goes). Home and End go to the first and last while the field is empty. With text in the field, Left and Right move the caret until it reaches the end it is heading for. Enter chooses. Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger.
Pressing a sticker with the mouse does not move the focus out of the search field, so with closeOnSelect off the arrow keys keep working between picks.
Each option is named by its sticker ("Rocket"); the count of matches is announced politely as you type ("12 stickers.", "No stickers found.").
The category chips are toggle buttons (aria-pressed) in their own tab stop; clicking one returns focus to the field. The row scrolls sideways on a narrow popover.
The highlighted sticker is shown by a highlighter swipe behind it, a small turn and the peeled corner, not by colour alone. Windows high contrast keeps the stickers (intrinsic art).
The empty state has a status line and Stubby with a magnifier.

items.name: sticker-sheet
items.title: Sticker sheet
items.description: A sheet of die-cut stickers on backing paper, each in its own kiss-cut outline. Press one and it peels away, drag one and it comes off under the mouse; the outline stays behind and can take it back. For reward charts, sticker packs and anything you collect.

a11y: The sheet is a named group; every sticker is a real button whose name changes with what pressing does ("Peel Rocket sticker" / "Put Rocket sticker back"). Enter and Space peel, exactly like a click.
What came off is announced politely ("Rocket peeled off.", "Rocket stuck back on."); the title shows how many are left.
While a sticker is in the hand the sheet rises above the rest of the page, so it can be carried over a board that comes after it in the source.

Dragging is a mouse and pen extra: touch never starts a drag (the page keeps scrolling), a tap peels. Every drag has a click or key equivalent, and releasing a drag near where it started springs the sticker back without peeling it.
The kiss-cut outlines and the printing are decoration (aria-hidden, no pointer events); the focus ring is drawn round the whole slot and never depends on colour alone.
Reduced motion: no flight or curl animation, the sticker is simply gone or back. Calm density: no sheen, no crop marks.
Windows high contrast keeps the stickers and outlines (intrinsic art).

items.name: sticker
items.title: Sticker
items.description: Die-cut vinyl stickers: the art with a white border, a cut line, a soft shadow and, if you like, a peeled corner. Status badges (done, sale) are generated; the rest are drawn by hand.

a11y: Decorative by default. A badge that carries meaning (Done, Sale) should sit next to real text or be given a `label`.

items.name: sticky-note
items.title: Sticky note
items.description: A square of coloured paper with a gum band, turned a little more than a page. Five pads, any size, written in marker. It can curl a corner, hang from a pin or a strip of tape, and grow a tick box that is ticked with a felt pen.

a11y: A note is a plain `div`. Give it `role="note"` or `as`-like semantics through props when it means more (for instance `role="group"` with an `aria-label` in a board of notes).

The gum band, curl, pin and tape are aria-hidden decoration. The tick box is drawing only unless you pass `onDoneChange`, and then it is a real checkbox (named by `doneLabel`, Space toggles, `aria-checked` follows `done`). A done note without it says "Done." to screen readers through hidden text; either way it is struck through, so meaning never rests on colour or the drawing alone.
Ink on every pad is at least 9:1; struck-through text switches to ink-soft (5.8:1 or better). Tilt is zero in calm density.
Sticky text is real DOM and wraps at any size (`break-words`), so a note resized by its container never clips.

items.name: strike
items.title: Strike
items.description: A red pencil through real words: one line, two lines, or a cross-out. The text stays readable and real underneath, so a price that was 49 can still be copied and read by a screen reader.

a11y: A real <s> element, which browsers and many screen readers treat as content that is no longer accurate. Say what changed in the surrounding text ("was", "now") rather than relying on the line alone.

When the line is only decoration (a ticked-off task whose state a checkbox already announces) use `asChild` on a <span>, so the words are not marked as deleted for everyone, and `show` for the on and off states; with `show={false}` the native line-through is hidden too.
The text underneath stays selectable and copyable; the drawing is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none.
Before the drawing exists and in Windows high contrast the browser's own line-through is shown.

items.name: switch
items.title: Switch
items.description: An on/off switch that is a marker pen being uncapped, not a glossy pill: a felt-outlined track the terracotta marker fills when it is on (with a darker rim where the ink pooled), and a paper coin for a thumb that slides across. Radix Switch underneath.

a11y: role="switch" with aria-checked true or false. Space and Enter toggle it, Tab focuses it (Radix). Label it with <Label htmlFor>, wrap it, or use aria-label.
State is not carried by colour alone: off shows a pencil o at the end and the thumb at the start, on shows a felt bar and the thumb at the end.
The hit area is 8 px larger than the track on every side (an ::after, so layout never moves). The track is 24 px tall at the default size, 20 px small with the enlarged hit area.
A Label beside it is a peer: peer-disabled dims it, and hovering the row (a `group/field`) or the label right after it lights the switch's hover overlay.

Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring; the drawing is aria-hidden, pointer-events: none and never focusable. Windows high contrast replaces the ink by a real border, a Highlight fill when on and a solid thumb.
Reduced motion (the OS setting or data-motion="reduced") makes the thumb jump and the marker appear at once.
Right-to-left: the thumb starts at the right and travels left (rtl: twins), and the o and bar marks swap ends.

items.name: table
items.title: Table
items.description: Rows and columns on a ruled page. Every rule is a pencil pull drawn once by the pen and printed by CSS (so a hundred rows cost no drawings), the header has an accountant's double rule, and a hovered or selected row is a highlighter swipe.

a11y: Real table semantics: table, rowgroup, columnheader, row, cell. Nothing is drawn inside the table elements; the rules and swipes are painted with CSS pseudo-elements and are invisible to assistive technology.

Mark the sorted column with `aria-sort="ascending" | "descending"` on its TableHead and put a `<button>` inside it (see the data table example); mark chosen rows with `data-state="selected"` and give their checkbox an accessible name.
Windows high contrast replaces the painted rules and swipe with real cell borders and the system highlight colours.
Hover only lights the swipe on pointers that can hover (and a row with an open menu, `aria-expanded`, stays lit). Reduced motion removes the fade.

Contrast on the swipe: ink is 11:1 on the full (selected) swipe, but green and red pencil text drop to about 4:1 there (4.7:1 on paper). Write status words in ink on selectable rows, as the data table example does, or keep coloured text out of them.
Calm density (`data-density="calm"`) draws straight hairline rules, a plain bold header and a flat swipe, for dense data.

items.name: tabs
items.title: Tabs
items.description: Index-divider tabs: the active one is lifted and filled with highlighter, and the pencil baseline breaks under it. Also a hairline `line` style with a blue felt underline, and vertical binder tabs. Radix behaviour and roving focus are untouched.

a11y: Radix roles and keys: tablist, tab (aria-selected, aria-controls) and tabpanel (aria-labelledby). Left/Right (Up/Down when vertical, mirrored in RTL) move between tabs and, in automatic mode, open them; Home and End jump to the first and last; Tab goes on into the panel.
The drawn tab, baseline and underline are aria-hidden and pointer-events: none; the tab keeps a 36 px hit box (32 compact, 28 calm).
The active tab is told apart by fill and outline, not by hue alone. Inactive text is 4.6:1 on paper, active text 14:1.
Keyboard focus draws a blue felt ring around the tab. Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with a real outline. Reduced motion turns the lift and the underline wipe into instant changes.
The tab list keeps its shape in right-to-left layouts: the vertical spine moves to the other side and the drawings mirror.

items.name: tally
items.title: Tally
items.description: A count as tally marks, 1 to 99: bundles of four struck through by a fifth. The number is the accessible name, the box is exactly as big as the marks, and it is drawn on the server.

a11y: role="img" with aria-label set to the number (or your label): a screen reader hears "7", not seven strokes. Add the counted thing in visible text nearby.
The marks are the only place the number is shown as a drawing, so the svg is kept in Windows high contrast (as system colours).
Right-to-left pages start the first bundle on the right.
Reduced motion zeroes the wipe.

items.name: tape
items.title: Tape
items.description: A strip of masking, washi, kraft or cellophane tape, drawn: translucent, with slit lines along its edges, crinkles and torn or pinked ends. Stick it across a corner, use it as a label, or let Paper place it for you.

a11y: Tape is decoration: aria-hidden, focusable=false, pointer-events: none. Never put the only copy of information on it; a label written on tape is real text next to (not inside) the svg.
Tape keeps its colours in Windows high contrast (it is an intrinsic ink kind).
Its tilt collapses to zero in calm density.

items.name: tear-off
items.title: Tear-off
items.description: A coupon, ticket or raffle strip with a stub you tear off along a perforated line. Pull the stub and it swings off its far corner, tap it or press Enter and it comes away; the ticket keeps a torn edge. Calls onTear once.

a11y: The stub is role="button" named by its text (or `label`) and described by "Press Enter or Space to tear it off along the dotted line, or pull it away with a pointer". Enter and Space tear it; pointer dragging is an extra, never the only way.
When it comes off the status line says "Torn off." politely, once; the stub then leaves the tab order and the accessibility tree.
Pointer: pull at least half way (or all the way) to tear; a shorter pull springs back; a tap tears; a cancelled pointer springs back.

Focus: when the stub is torn off with the keyboard, focus moves to the ticket itself (it becomes programmatically focusable, with no ring), so Tab carries on from the ticket instead of restarting at the top of the page. Keys typed in something inside the stub never tear it.
Reduced motion: the stub does not swing or fall, it is simply gone. Right-to-left layouts put the stub on the left and pull it that way.
The perforation and the scissors are decoration (aria-hidden). Calm density leaves the scissors out and keeps the dashes.

items.name: textarea
items.title: Textarea
items.description: A multi-line text field on paper: a pencil box around a real <textarea> that grows with its text, with optional hand-ruled lines on the baselines, a drawn resize handle and a character counter.

a11y: A native <textarea>: Enter adds a line, Tab moves on, and label / aria-describedby / required work as usual.
aria-invalid, disabled and readOnly are the real attributes; the drawing follows them.
Focus draws the blue felt ring; the browser's outline is used before the drawing exists and in Windows high contrast.
The counter is aria-describedby text ("12 characters of 280"), never a live region.
Resizing uses the browser's own handle (made transparent and redrawn by hand), so it keeps working with the mouse and touch.
field-sizing: content needs a current browser; elsewhere the textarea keeps its rows and scrolls.

items.name: ticket
items.title: Ticket
items.description: A ticket with concave corners, a bite out of both edges where the stub tears off, and a row of holes along the tear. The holes are cut out of the paper, so the desk (and the shadow) show through. A body, a stub, spaced capitals in the typewriter font and a serial number in red.

a11y: A ticket is a `div`. Give it `role="group"` and a label when several sit on a page. The stub is an `aside` with `role="note"`, so a page of tickets does not fill up with unnamed complementary landmarks.

The drawn paper, notches, holes and frames are aria-hidden decoration; the ticket's information is text in the body and stub. Punched is shown by a hole and a data attribute: also say it in text ("Used") if it matters.

Ink on every ticket stock is at least 9:1; the serial number is a red darkened with ink and reads at least 4.9:1 on kraft, yellow and pink. The tilt is zero in calm density; Windows high contrast replaces the drawing with an outline.

items.description: A row of toggles that belong together: pick one (alignment) or several (bold, italic, underline). Joined outline items share one hand-drawn box with a pencil seam between them; the highlighter body marks what is on.

single is announced as a radio group with checked items; multiple as a toolbar of pressed buttons. Give the group an aria-label and every icon-only item its own.
On is never told by hue alone: a filled body sits under the item, and (separate items) a solid box replaces the whisper box.
The focus ring is drawn on the item and lifted above its neighbours; Windows high contrast falls back to real borders and the browser's focus ring.
In right-to-left layouts the seams move to the other edge; the drawing is mirrored by the recipe, not by CSS.

items.name: tooltip
items.title: Tooltip
items.description: A sticky note stuck next to a control, with a felt-tip arrow pointing at it. It names an icon button or adds a hint, opens on hover and keyboard focus with a shared delay, and never hides anything a person needs to be able to read.

a11y: Radix Tooltip: the note has role=tooltip and the trigger gets `aria-describedby` while it is open; the text is announced as the trigger's description. It opens on hover and on keyboard focus, and Escape closes it.

Tooltips never open on a touch tap (Radix ignores touch pointers) and are not focusable themselves: never put the only copy of a label, an instruction or an error in one. An icon button still needs an `aria-label`.
A disabled button does not receive pointer or focus events, so it cannot show a tooltip: wrap it in a focusable element (see the example) if the reason it is disabled matters.
The arrow is aria-hidden decoration. Note text is ink on sticky yellow (about 12:1). With reduced motion the note appears without the zoom; in `calm` density it is a flat, untilted note.
Portalled content repeats the InkProvider's `data-density`, `data-motion` and `data-theme`.

items.name: typewriter
items.title: Typewriter
items.description: Text that types itself in the typewriter face, with an inked caret. Keys land at uneven speeds and hold at commas and full stops; several phrases can go one under the other or be typed, held and backspaced in turn.

a11y: Screen readers get the whole text once, from a visually hidden polite live region; they never hear it letter by letter. The typed copy is aria-hidden. Changing `text` is announced once.
In cycle mode and when looping the live region is off, so a rotating word is not announced on every turn; the phrases are all available as one sentence in reading order.
Reduced motion (the OS setting, data-motion="reduced", or an InkProvider with motion="reduced"): no typing, no blinking; the finished text (the last phrase of a cycle) is shown.
Without JavaScript the server has already sent the whole text in the page.

Layout: by default the element grows as it types, so anything below it moves. Pass `reserve` to hold the room of the finished text from the first frame (an invisible copy in flow, aria-hidden, that no one can select), or give a block of several lines a `min-h-*`. It is made for a headline or a few short lines: every key press re-renders the words typed so far, so do not feed it pages of text.
One key press is one character as a person sees it: an emoji, a flag or a letter with its accent is typed and erased whole, never in halves.

Words sit up to a pixel off the baseline and a shade lighter, as plain inline text (a word with a layer of its own was cut at its advance by WebKit, which clipped the tail of a hand font's last glyph); calm density and reduced motion turn the jitter off through --ll-jitter-k.

items.name: typing-indicator
items.title: Typing indicator
items.description: "Somebody is writing": a small pencil that draws three dots one after another, or scrawls a line of cursive. A polite live region with a screen-reader label, at home inside a bubble.

a11y: `role="status"` with `aria-live="polite"`: it never interrupts. The label is visually hidden text; the drawing is an aria-hidden svg.

A live region announces changes, not arrivals: keep the indicator mounted and toggle `active` (the examples do) instead of mounting it when someone starts typing. Keep it exposed too: `hidden`, `display: none` or `visibility: hidden` on an ancestor removes the region from the accessibility tree, so collapse the bubble around it with `sr-only`.
The animation is decoration. With `prefers-reduced-motion` (or the app's calm setting) every animation ends on its last frame, which is the complete drawing; nothing blinks or loops.
Ink on paper is 14:1 (blue felt 7.1:1); the marks are not the only carrier of meaning, the label is.

items.name: typography
items.title: Typography
items.description: The type scale and a Prose wrapper for the notebook: script headings with a hand-drawn rule, body text in the hand at 17 px on a 1.7 line, blue felt links, marker bullets, mono code chips. Prose styles markup you did not write (markdown, CMS html, MDX).

a11y: Real elements with their real semantics: h1 to h4, p, ul/ol, blockquote, code. Nothing here changes the outline or the reading order.

Body text is the hand at 17 px in ink on paper (14:1); muted text is the muted-foreground token (4.5:1 or better on paper and on the desk); links are blue felt (7:1) and bold with a thick underline, never colour alone.
The hand-drawn heading rule is a baked alpha mask painted by ::after; browsers without mask support keep a plain pencil border. Windows high contrast paints the rule with system text colour.
Line length is capped at 64 characters in Prose; long words wrap and code blocks scroll sideways (a table wider than the column needs a scrolling wrapper of its own).

items.name: underline
items.title: Underline
items.description: A pen line under real words: single, double, wavy or scribbled, in felt, pencil or marker. It follows the phrase line by line when it wraps, and can draw itself on as it scrolls into view.

a11y: The words are ordinary text: selectable, copyable, found by search. The line is aria-hidden and pointer-events-none.
Until the drawing exists (no JavaScript, first paint) and in Windows high contrast, the browser's own text-decoration underline is shown in the pen's colour.
Do not use it as the only sign of a link: put it on a real <a> with asChild (links keep their native focus ring) or keep the link's own underline.
Reduced motion (or data-motion="reduced") zeroes the draw-on.

items.description: A sidebar with a popover: a notes app with favorites and workspaces on the pad and, in the page header, a star and a "..." that opens a slip of actions built from the same menu parts as the pad. Mirrors shadcn's sidebar-10. Looks right on the desk and on plain paper.

items.name: sidebar-shared
items.title: Sidebar parts
items.description: The pieces the sixteen sidebar blocks share: brand header, search box, team switcher, account menu, project and secondary lists, folding calendars, a page header with breadcrumbs, and the small hand-written note that stands where content goes. It installs by itself with any sidebar block; copy the parts you like into your app.

items.name: signup-01
items.title: Signup 01
items.description: A guest check on the desk: a paper clip, dashed tear lines top and bottom, and a member number in the corner. Name, email, password twice and a Google button, with live messages in the fields. Made for the desk.
items.docs:
Installed the "Signup 01" block into your components directory under blocks/signup-01/.
Import it: import Signup01Page from "<your components alias>/blocks/signup-01/page"
Needs @hookform/resolvers@^5, react-hook-form@^7, zod@^4: the CLI installs them (a project on an older major is upgraded).
